q: Why do tile makers in Castellon and Sassuolo pay for carbon while imported tiles do not?
title: EU tile makers vs imported tiles
short: Ceramic kilns in the EU with a capacity above 75 tonnes a day are covered by the EU ETS, so they buy allowances for emissions above their free allocation. Ceramic tiles are not in Annex I of the CBAM Regulation, so tiles imported from India, China or Turkey carry no CBAM charge.
audience: Tile makers in the Castellon and Sassuolo districts, and tile exporters selling into the EU

p: Annex I of the EU ETS Directive lists the manufacture of ceramic products by firing, including tiles, with a production capacity above 75 tonnes a day. Those plants monitor and verify their emissions and surrender allowances each year.
CBAM covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity. Ceramic tiles under chapter 69 are not on the list, so an importer of tiles has no CBAM declaration to make.

EU buyers counting Scope 3, green building schemes asking for environmental product declarations, and product rules under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation can still ask for a tile's footprint. A Morbi or Castellon tile with a documented figure per square metre is easier to specify.
